body.text: Three continental gatherings on the Egyptian coast offer India a strategic window to deepen its engagement with Africa

From 2 to 4 October 2026, the Mediterranean coastal city of New Alamein will temporarily transform into the geopolitical and economic capital of the African continent. Egypt is set to host a high-profile trio of continental gatherings: the inaugural Alamein Africa Forum 2026 on investment, the summit of the founding states of the African Union Development Agency (AUDA-NEPAD), and the African Union’s eighth mid-year coordination meeting. With heads of state, development financiers, and global business leaders convening on the Egyptian coast, Cairo is sending a clear, unequivocal message about its leadership role in driving African economic integration.

For New Delhi, this convergence of continental leadership should not be viewed merely as a distant diplomatic spectacle. Instead, it is a strategic window of opportunity. As India looks to deepen its footprint in the Global South and secure its economic future amid shifting global supply chains, the momentum generating in New Alamein offers the perfect catalyst to elevate India-Africa cooperation. In this new era, Egypt serves as the indispensable geographic and economic bridge.

In recent years, the relationship between India and Egypt has experienced a renaissance. President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi’s 2023 state visit produced the decision to elevate ties to a strategic partnership covering political, security, defence, economic and scientific cooperation. The bilateral economic fundamentals are undeniably strong. Trade hovered around US$6.5 billion in recent fiscal years, and robust investments from Indian enterprises spanning technology, pharmaceuticals, and manufacturing continue to pour into the Egyptian market. The two governments also expressed the objective of raising bilateral trade to US$12 billion within five years. However, viewing Cairo strictly through the lens of a bilateral partner artificially limits its geopolitical utility. Egypt’s true potential for India lies not just in its domestic market of over 100 million people, but in its unique positioning at the strategic crossroads of Africa, Asia, and Europe.

The traditional model of India-Africa cooperation - historically built on the noble pillars of capacity building, lines of credit, and anti-colonial solidarity - must now evolve into complex, trilateral economic partnerships. Egypt is the ideal catalyst for this transition for three distinct and compelling reasons.

The traditional model of India-Africa cooperation - historically built on the noble pillars of capacity building, lines of credit, and anti-colonial solidarity - must now evolve into complex, trilateral economic partnerships. Egypt is the ideal catalyst for this transition.

First, Egypt offers unmatched logistical connectivity and an established gateway to the continent's burgeoning markets. A primary challenge for Indian businesses attempting to scale their presence in Africa has been the continent's fragmented infrastructure and complex tariff barriers. Egypt provides a sophisticated workaround. Through the Suez Canal Economic Zone (SCZONE) and Egypt's membership in the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) - the largest free trade area in the world by the number of participating countries - Indian manufacturers can establish production hubs on Egyptian soil. By manufacturing or assembling in Egypt, Indian firms in sectors like automotives, pharmaceuticals, and agro-processing can access broader African markets with zero or significantly reduced tariffs. This strategic positioning allows Indian businesses to bypass the infrastructural bottlenecks that often hinder direct bilateral trade with sub-Saharan nations, effectively creating a highly resilient supply chain that links Indian innovation to African consumption, while keeping European markets within arm's reach.

Second, the structural priorities of the New Alamein summits currently underway - specifically mobilising resources, advancing regional economic integration, and building resilient partnerships - align seamlessly with India’s core developmental strengths. Africa is currently on the cusp of a massive demographic and digital transition. By 2050, an estimated 1.3 billion people on the continent will be under the age of thirty. India, which has navigated similar developmental imperatives and demographic youth bulges, is uniquely positioned to share its scalable, tested solutions. Trilateral cooperation driven by Indian technology and Egyptian regional influence can dramatically accelerate the deployment of Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) across the continent. India’s success with the Unified Payments Interface (UPI), biometric identity, and accessible telemedicine provides a blueprint for African nations seeking to leapfrog traditional development hurdles. By partnering with Egyptian institutions, which possess a deep understanding of regional regulatory and cultural nuances, Indian tech firms can localise and scale these digital solutions, transforming financial inclusion and healthcare delivery.

Third, both India and Egypt share a critical, existential interest in the green energy transition and the development of sustainable infrastructure. As Africa industrialises, there is a global imperative to ensure this growth does not replicate the carbon-heavy trajectories of the past. Frustrated by the unfulfilled climate finance promises of the developed world, the Global South is increasingly looking inward for solutions. Egypt has proactively positioned itself as a future hub for green hydrogen and renewable-energy-powered industrial clusters, capitalising on its abundant solar and wind resources. India, a leader in the International Solar Alliance with rapidly growing technological expertise in clean energy, is a natural partner in this endeavour. By aligning Indian green capital and engineering prowess with Egypt's strategic location and natural resources, both nations can jointly power African industrialisation. Trilateral ventures in solar grid connectivity, electric vehicle manufacturing, and green hydrogen production can establish a new paradigm for sustainable development.

By explicitly leveraging the India-Egypt Strategic Partnership as a continental launchpad, New Delhi can shift its African engagement into a cohesive, integrated strategy. The road to a robust, future-proof India-Africa partnership runs directly through Cairo.

The three-day diplomatic intensive in New Alamein serves as a potent reminder that Africa is rapidly consolidating its economic architecture and taking charge of its development narrative. The continent is no longer just seeking aid; it is actively seeking equitable partnerships, investment, and technological integration. If India wants to be a foundational partner in the next chapter of the African growth story, it needs reliable, capable, and influential anchor states on the continent. By explicitly leveraging the India-Egypt Strategic Partnership as a continental launchpad, New Delhi can shift its African engagement into a cohesive, integrated strategy. The road to a robust, future-proof India-Africa partnership runs directly through Cairo. It is time for Indian policymakers to recognise Egypt not just as a lucrative destination, but as the primary catalyst for a shared, prosperous future.

Hindol Sengupta is Professor of International Relations and Executive Dean at the Jindal School of International Affairs (JSIA), O.P. Jindal Global University, and Director of the Jindal India Institute.

Hebatallah Adam is Professor of International Economics, Academic Dean, Founder and Director of Jindal Centre for the Global South, at the Jindal School of International Affairs (JSIA), O.P. Jindal Global University.
